utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry about the late start this afternoon, but I gather the earlier trial again overran in circumstances that were not foreseen. What I propose this afternoon is that we deal first of all with the balance of the argument over the amendment to the 65 ter summary in respect of the next witness. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may address that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Given the nature of the issue, Your Honour, since Mr. Stamp and I are the senior trial attorneys on this case and we're ultimately responsible for the things that happened wrong or -- hopefully we'll get some credit for the things that go right, but we have to accept the responsibility, ultimately it's ours to shoulder and so I feel I should speak to it as opposed to Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure where we left off yesterday when you asked us to do some further investigation. I can tell you we have done some. It is an error on our part. It is something that perhaps should have been in there but wasn't. But I would indicate this was a 92 bis witness, 92 bis (D). The package included both his prior testimony and both his statements in which this material is contained. The 92 bis request was granted and this witness was required to come for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you talk about the 92 bis (D) package, though, you're talking in jargon in respect of the timing of notice, I understand that that's how you present it to the Court. But are you saying that in some way there was a package delivered to the Defence at a much earlier stage that would easily have alerted them to the fact that you intended to refer to two statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. When we originally disclosed the statements and the transcript to the original three MOS defendants in January of 2003, in May -- I'm sorry, June 30th of 2005, the most recent three indictees were provided that discovery. The 92 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- package was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's general disclosure or is this supporting material for the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This was Rule 66 disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But when we filed the 92 bis package in association with your 92 bis motion that we filed with the Court, that was filed on the 20th of May this year -- the 26th of May, I'm sorry. And on the 4th of July is when Your Honours ruled on the -- the motion and agreed with our position that this material was appropriate for treatment as 92 bis for in addition, but the witnesses would be required to attend for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me be clear about these various things. Are you saying that the transcript which plainly refers to the two statements was disclosed under 66(A)(i) as part of the supporting material for the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think it was only disclosed under 66(A)(ii).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was apprehensive after yesterday that this might not be an isolated problem. If you have failed in other areas also to update the 65 ter summary from the Milosevic trial, we would effectively have 65 ter material frozen as at 2001. Now, ought we to be fearful that that may be the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in light of what has happened up to this date, I have some concerns about that and we are engaged in the process of reviewing all 65 ters because of what has occurred recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, I made a general statement of anxiety yesterday about the way in which a number of witnesses appear to be being presented on the basis of very historical material, as if no one had had a serious look at it since 2002 when all the Kosovo witnesses seem to have given evidence in the Milosevic trial. And that disturbed me, obviously, because of the effort that I thought had been made by everyone to -- in the course of the pre-trial work to streamline the case. Now, what you're really saying to me is, if you don't know the answer to the question whether this is a common problem, that you don't really have an explanation for why it's happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in this particular case, Your Honour, again -- I guess this is a matter that I would ask Your Honours to leave to me and our office in particular to deal with because it's -- it's a matter that we have to resolve internally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's got wider implications than that, Mr. Hannis. If it's a serious problem, then it will need to be addressed by the Court, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, ultimately I'm sure that that's true, Your Honour, if we don't correct the problem. If it continues to be a problem, then I would agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The original 65 ter summary for this case identifies the witness as speaking to two paragraphs of the indictment that don't really make the position remotely clear. In paragraph 16 of this indictment is a very general one-sentence paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I'm looking at the wrong version. I'm looking at the witness notification that makes reference to paragraph 72(b) and (d) and 75(d). Are you looking at a 65 ter from May of 2000?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 10th of May --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have that before me. And that may have been -- I don't know if paragraph 16 changed after that date when we amended the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The one thing it does do -- well, one thing you can rely on about it is that it refers to Rule 92 bis (D) giving clear notice that it's the transcript that's the foundation of the evidence for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in Milosevic, as you know, most of those witnesses who appeared, their 92 -- their statements were put in under 92 bis (B) as part of the 92 bis (D) evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you have a matter that needs urgent attention, Mr. Hannis. And by what I mean the -- the question whether there's a general problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will give it that urgent attention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I may come back to you once we hear what has to be said by the Defence. Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- I sometimes rise with trepidation because I make representations based upon the state of my preparation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I -- can I maybe assist by indicating what -- having a -- having read through the -- all the papers that might be relevant, at least that I think are relevant, I have established -- there is one paragraph of the indictment which says quite a bit about what this evidence relates to, and I think it is 75(d).

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in that, there's a reference to both of these burial sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I don't contest that, and I don't contest that it's part of the indictment and I don't contest that the Prosecution has a right to put on this evidence. I contest none of those things. What I'm concerned about is, is the question of notice and whether these 65 ter summaries have any effect at all or not or whether we should start ignoring them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can I say that I think this particular event has identified the possibility of a more widespread problem, but we're going to find that out later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would prefer to deal with this issue in the knowledge of the width of its spread through the 65 ter notice. So far as this witness is concerned, my own provisional view at the moment is that there is enough indication by reference to the witness being a 92 bis (D) witness, therefore transcript which includes two statements, plus the terms of this paragraph of the indictment, to say that it would be quite difficult to refuse to hear this evidence. But as with the previous case, if you were to indicate a particular difficulty in dealing with cross-examination, then we would be sympathetic to any motion for adjournment and possibly preferably re-call of the witness in the circumstances. But looking at this one as an isolated example, my inclination would be to allow the evidence to be led, subject to anything else that's said. If there's a broader problem, I would not regard that as having established any precedent for dealing with the broader issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I started in my remarks, that I think the Prosecution has every right to call this evidence. It's not a question of whether in my mind but a question of when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It may be my error, and it very well could be, but it just never occurred to me until this document was handed to me yesterday that I should look into this matter and be prepared to cross-examine on this matter, and it probably should have but it didn't. The other thing -- and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I think -- the reason I say I think this one is exceptional is because that paragraph of the indictment is so specific. It's one of the -- it's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the flip-side of the other problem that we had earlier in the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The other -- the other issue, Your Honour, is that unless again I am just deficient in my preparation, I know I am in many respects, we were given I think yesterday a brand new statement of this witness that was given on 16 May 2005 to a judge from a court in Belgrade. And you've seen one of these statements at least before. We got it only in B/C/S. I have sent it off for translation to CLSS, asking them to rush it as much as possible. I am told by people on my staff that read B/C/S that -- that there are some matters in here that I would want to be aware of before I cross-examine this witness. And of course, as you know, Your Honour, in the process of cross-examination from a document like this you need to be pretty precise. You can't just say: My colleague told me this says such and such, and ask a question on that basis. So I wouldn't oppose this witness being called; I would simply ask that he be called at some later date, maybe 30 days from now, and that would give everybody a chance to investigate this paragraph that was added yesterday plus a chance to look at this new statement and see what impact it might have on cross-examination. But I can tell you, I'm -- with this I'm not prepared to go forward and cross-examine this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The new statement is news to me. It must be simply as a piece of disclosure to you rather than something that's to be used as part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. This is something the witness brought with him when he came. It's his testimony in a state court proceeding in these same matters that we didn't have until -- we didn't know existed until he brought it and gave it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Ackerman, whether the next -- I think there are two other witnesses who may be available this week. Do you know if they are likely to give rise to problems of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't think so until 1.30 when we received a brand new supplemental information sheet for this -- for that witness. At 1.30 today. I mean, I'm just -- luckily I was looking at my computer instead of riding my bicycle to court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's Mr. Zogaj, Shefqet Zogaj, and I'm going to be frank, Your Honour. I think the problem is we are all working beyond our capacity in many ways. I'm getting so tired I can barely stand and talk to you because we're working so many hours and the Prosecution is doing the same thing. I'm not blaming the Prosecution for being late with these things. I think they're doing the best they can. We're just operating under such pressure that it's affecting -- things are getting -- spiraling out of control here. We think we need to get a little bit better organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll not comment too quickly on where you think the blame lies, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Hannis, this is beginning to prevent, I think, progress at the moment. It sounds as though -- in fact, is Mr. Zogaj the next witness or is he next but one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Gjogaj, G-j-o.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Z-o-g-a-j I think?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, would be the next one and after him a Mr. Zogaj --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Zogaj I think -- give me a second until I find the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shefqet Zogaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which is the witness that you've disclosed another supplementary sheet for?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's Mr. Zogaj. He brought with him materials that we had not seen before when he was proofed this morning. Your Honour, this week we're running a day behind in terms of when our witnesses are arriving because of the anticipated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So Ali Gjogaj, there's no problem with?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He's here and ready to go, but that's the one we have the problem with the amended 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sorry. And then Zogaj is -- what about Fondaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fondaj, Your Honour, was supposed to arrive yesterday. I received an email last night saying she was not on the plane. She was travelling with a support person and there were only -- there was only one seat available. She would not travel without her support person, so she's not arriving until 10.00 tonight. She's never testified before, she's not been proofed, Your Honour, and if we have a morning session tomorrow, I found that I was going to be in a difficult position to put her on without any proofing or being proofed at 7.00 in the morning after being in bed at midnight on her first trip to The Hague. Your Honour, I would like to suggest rather than rescheduling Mr. Gjogaj, because the Defence has had both his statements and his transcript, we proceed with him today. If it turns out that there are real problems because of the state court transcript that he brought with him, perhaps he could be called back at a later date for cross-examination, but it may evolve that it won't be necessary. I suggest that is the way to try and salvage some of the time this week. I'm sorry, it's a statement, not a transcript from the state court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is a statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it's not something you're relying on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. We only have it in B/C/S. It hasn't been translated yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what about the supplementary material for the next witness after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp may be able to address that. He proofed him this morning and can tell you what the nature of that material is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stamp, is that material you'll be relying upon?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The material, although it's quite extensive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It will not be material that we are relying on. It is -- it is -- it relates to the contents of his proposed testimony, but the -- there are three books that he has recently written about his testimony before the ICTY and they are -- the matters that he witnessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, does anyone have any separate point to make from those made by Mr. Ackerman? Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Simply on this witness, Zogaj, I'm just looking at it now, the additional material, I have not seen it. And it's -- it's really very extensive. Now, Mr. Stamp might not be relying on it because I think quite frankly it has overwhelmed him. It is a huge bunch of material, including books he's written on the very one of -- the very subjects that he's going to be testifying about today and there could be information in there that could be very important to this case. That's what concerns me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am -- I think we're all sympathetic to that, but when witnesses have travelled and are available and we can take the evidence in chief and any cross-examination that counsel feel able to conduct, then it seems not unreasonable to do that. I don't see how that will prejudice the situation, and indeed it may be that we could say we expect you to carry out the cross-examination that you are prepared to carry out and indicate clearly that we will be sympathetic to the re-call of the witness should you demonstrate that there is more that you ought to have been in a position to ask if you'd been given the material in adequate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I think we will take up the proposal of Mr. Hannis to proceed on that basis. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just say this. If there is material that I have not had a chance to look at in terms of preparing cross-examination, it would be foolish for me to do a partial cross-examination because that material may completely change the whole approach one takes to a cross. So I have no objection to these witnesses being brought and put on for direct examination, but I don't think anyone should be asked to do any cross-examination until they've seen all this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that decision ought to be left to individual counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And others may have different views of how they perceive the witness, but I hear what you say and we'll consider the decision just in a moment and give you a final ruling on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I should say something. First of all, you said something, one particular word, which with all due respect I did not like, Mr. President, and that is to see who is to be blamed for what happened. I believe that the Prosecution cannot be blamed at all. You see, I do not see the Prosecutors as people who came here to do something that is not right. It's going to happen to us too, you know, it's going to happen to us as well and then we're going to seek your understanding just as I have understanding for them now. I mean, I'm sorry, Your Honour, Judge Bonomy, it seems to me I'm telling you something that is -- well, sort of something wrong, something that I shouldn't be saying to you. But it's not the consequence that's a problem. I mean, why would I believe that any one of the ladies and gentlemen of the Prosecution did not want to show this to us earlier on and they could have? You see, we have a war crimes tribunal in Belgrade that is working at full throttle and almost all these witnesses that you're going to hear here are being heard in Belgrade as well. So let us deal with the cause rather than the effect. I'm sorry to have risen. I'm sorry to take up your time. But let us not deal with the effect. What you're doing now, Your Honour, is resolving the effect of this. You are resolving the problem of how I'm going to deal with my high temperature because I have a cold, whereas I want to resolve the basic problem, I want to prevent a cold. Now, let's see what the ladies and gentlemen of the Prosecution suggest. How can we avoid this kind of situation from happening once again, in your case and in our case, because it's going to happen to us, too, you see. You know, there is something I don't like about your system. I watched the Milosevic trial and some witness called Aleksovski was heard there. And then all of a sudden Mr. Nice was bothered by Aleksovski talking about other witnesses as second-hand evidence, hearsay - you were there yourself, Your Honour - and before that he was not bothered by hearing hearsay witnesses during his own case. I don't want to take up too much time, but let's have these common rules of courtesy on both sides. Let us not lay blame anywhere. Because if I believe that any one of the ladies and gentlemen from the Prosecution wanted to do something on purpose, that would have been terrible, and that would be impermissible. Let us try and find a solution, let us try to see, say, that they be given all the records from the Belgrade court. There's nothing wrong with that whatsoever because in Belgrade all these people were heard a long time ago and this is probably going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina, too, as well. For example, I heard about the Celebici trial, the way that it ended here is now being repeated in Sarajevo -- well, I don't mean that it's totally being repeated but parts of it are being repeated. So let us look at all of this. Please, Your Honour, deal with the cause. As for the effect, yes, I agree with you. Once these people have arrived, yes, let's hear them, yes, but let's not have this repeated. I'm sorry, I've really taken up a lot of your time, but believe me, I rise to my feet with every good intention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I am the first to acknowledge that there has been goodwill displayed on both sides throughout the preparation for and conduct of this trial and I've said so before. I'm not simply saying so in response to your comments and I don't for a minute suggest that there's any bad faith involved in anything that's happened, so you can be re-assured on that score. However, I've spent already more than two years in this case as a Pre-Trial Judge, and I thought that things were being done by the Prosecution to streamline it. I've already said this morning -- this afternoon, I will not make any judgement on where blame might lie, but I may have to make that judgement in due course, depending on the explanation that's given to me and the consequences that are -- that flow from that explanation. I'm relieved to some extent to hear what has been said by the Defence this afternoon; it's very re-assuring. But if in fact the events of the last two days were to be repeated on a wholesale scale throughout the list of witnesses in this case, then it may be that we have to have a major re-think of the trial and that, I'm afraid, may have quite unacceptable repercussions. So it's too early, I accept, to make any final judgement on the situation. I don't accept that at this moment you can simply say: This is an inevitable consequence of a case of this nature. I mentioned yesterday that an instrument that we've had for more than a century, the telephone, and the one that we've had for - I don't know, is it approaching 30 years? - the fax, and I've just invited the Prosecution to perhaps think using methods they haven't been using so far to solve a problem that's arisen. I'm conscious of the need also to solve the immediate problem. However, we'll hear more about these various issues at a later stage. We'll consider these submissions and decide what action to take in relation to the next two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in relation to the witness Ali Gjogaj, we will allow amendment of the Rule 65 ter notice. We will proceed to hear the evidence in chief. If that's concluded today, we would invite counsel to endeavour to be in a position to deal with cross-examination because so far as that witness is concerned it's one statement we're talking about. What's the length of the statement, then, Ms. Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're dealing with a five-page statement that is predominantly spaced-out, that includes the cover page and the final --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I understand urgent efforts being made to get an understanding of that statement on the part of the Defence. Is that right, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know how it got into a five-page statement. I've got one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, a little over eight pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, when you said the second statement, I thought you were referring the second statement that's part of the 92 bis package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: He is speaking to the Belgrade statement, and he is correct. It ends up being and ERN range from K0532529 through 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Jargon again, Ms. Carter. Just the number of pages, please. I'm a simple-minded person.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: It is eight pages of text, Your Honour. It is double that, but it just ends up being a stamp on it without any material on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand efforts were made to get a rapid translation of this. You can only do your best, I'm not suggesting otherwise, but I'm trying to advance a compromise here which would involve the witness being examined today and, if possible, cross-examined tomorrow, and then proceeding to the examination-in-chief of the next witness, that's Shefqet Zogaj on the basis that that cross-examination could not be undertaken at all at this stage and would be postponed until a suitable opportunity and it would be for the Defence to advise the court of the date of that, since I understand we're talking about a journalist writing a number of books in Albanian, which it would take some time to digest through translation. Now, can we try that? And I appreciate, we may not achieve the objective because of the difficulty of getting a quick translation of the statement, but bear in mind -- or we bear in mind that the accused here and many of the counsel here will be able to read that statement in the form in which they have it. And therefore, I was hoping that all -- by acting together you might be in a position to cross-examine tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- if CLSS moves at their fastest pace, it will be available sometime tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably after we've finished, but you do make a good suggestion otherwise. It may be that I have colleagues here who read this language very well who will conduct a cross-examination that I would eventually be satisfied with, having read this statement later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the suggestion --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That may work and it may be that I won't even ask that this person be brought back or I won't have any additional cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We appreciate that the position is different with the journalist. So that's how we'll deal with the questions of the evidence. Now, I want to do two other things since Mr. Hannis is here. Just give me a moment. There are two related motions before the Trial Chamber. The most recent of these is a joint Defence motion to compel Rule 68 disclosure, and that -- that motion flows from an order the Trial Chamber made on the 15th of August which was seen at the time as -- it was seen at the time as a rather technical exercise because it granted certain protective measures to material which was being disclosed to the Prosecution under Rule 70 and which the Prosecution sought to disclose to the Defence. And the assumption -- not just the assumption, the declared position of the Prosecution was that they had been authorised to disclose it to the Defence as long as this protection was granted by the Court. And the subsequent motion has now come in because the material has not been disclosed. Now, before we get involved in the bureaucratic exercise of going through, waiting for a response, writing a decision, can you help us, Mr. Hannis, on the current situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We have disclosed that material today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much. The second matter related to that was -- I'm sorry, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know, I mean what Mr. Hannis meant, but this material that was disclosed to us today was in actual fact disclosed to us on earlier occasions, several earlier occasions. What we got today is actually a copy of material that was previously disclosed to us by the Prosecution. What we expect to receive from them is material that hasn't been disclosed to us to this day, and they were supposed to ask the relevant governments for that. I'm not going to give the names of the witnesses to whom this applies, but obviously we are asked for even more than originally requested. And also, we would like to have direct communication with the OTP in this respect. However, it is my understanding that the material disclosed to us today is certainly not what we were expecting to receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in case of any confusion, though, in your mind, Mr. Visnjic, the other matter I was about to raise was your motion to exclude the testimony of witnesses for failure to comply with disclosure obligations. Now, I suspect that that's what you're addressing at the moment -- it's not what you're addressing?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Inter alia I'm talking about that, too, because in addition to those witnesses -- I mean, I'm expecting some more material pertaining to other things. But inter alia, that is included in what I said a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, can you help me any further on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. Maybe I have to sit and talk directly with Mr. Visnjic, but what we disclosed today, it is material that the original three had been disclosed previously. What we had been waiting before was permission from the Prosecution to disclose that same material to the three new accused in this case. We got that permission, and today we disclosed that to them. But to try and avoid confusion, even though there was some duplication, we disclosed everything to everybody, even though the original MOS defendants had received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that motion, that particular motion, was confined to giving authority so that you could disclose to the third -- the fourth, fifth, and sixth accused what had already been disclosed to the first, second, and third accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, the separate matter then is the -- the motion to exclude the testimony of certain witnesses for failure to comply with disclosure obligations, and that motion includes among its averments that on the 17th of August, 2006, counsel for General Ojdanic, that's Mr. Visnjic, was informed by - and that's the country in question - that it had not yet received a formal request from the OTP for the testimony of that witness. Now, have -- have matters moved on at all since then?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: They have, Your Honour. I have to talk a little bit about procedure in connection with this. This is one that initially we had a delay in putting names on our witness list because we were trying to get privilege from provider. We did that. Then we had to request the opportunity to interview those individuals, which was done prior to the 17th of August. At that time, then we sent our draft, former request, because we were asked to proceed in that fashion so we can be advised whether there were any problems with our request. Today -- yesterday, the formal request went out, I contacted the provider's representative today to try and get a timetable on how long it would be before we can get approval. I was told three weeks as an optimistic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm conscious that Mr. Fila might think we are being unduly pre-emptory in our approach to matters, but we are not prepared to allow this sort of situation to drift indefinitely. And it may be that if the matter is to be addressed formally by the Trial Chamber, the state in question should be given an opportunity of responding to this motion. Or are you content, Mr. Hannis, that you can give the Trial Chamber all the information it will require to make a decision on the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I can provide you that information, Your Honour, and I think I have crossed all the biggest hurdles as of this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, Mr. Visnjic, if we decide to postpone our decision on this motion for three weeks on the basis that you understand we are anxious to make a final decision about this so that everyone knows where they stand, is that acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid that with regard to this particular matter that we've just discussed there is yet additional documentation on our side, and I would like to ask you for a shorter deadline, a day or two. I would like to submit that to you. This is our own correspondence with some of these states. So could you then please rule on delaying your own decision with regard to our original request. So could we say do this by Monday at the latest? Can I submit to you our entire correspondence that we had with regard to the provision of documents with individual states and then you will see what the situation is. And this has to do with the explanation just provided to you by Mr. Hannis. Just give me three days. I agree in principle, if you accept our additional documentation that I would like to provide to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have absolutely no problem accepting your additional documentation on a matter like this. All I'm wanting to be clear about is that if we give an indication that we're anxious to reach a final decision, a definitive decision, but feel that three weeks is not an unreasonable time in all the circumstances to allow Mr. Hannis, in view of all that's happened, then if you give us that indication we can file this for the moment and make our decision after he has had his three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask you to wait with your decision -- I mean giving him three weeks. Do not grant him that before you get our documents. I think I've been very specific now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So you want to file more material by Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you proceed to do that. We will not make any decision on this until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, I think that completes a need for your presence and can we turn to Ms. Carter and the witness Berisha --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, yes, of course, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for the witness to go, there's perhaps another ancillary matter I could raise. It's just to put something on the record. When the witness has testified there is an issue in respect to the transcript pages and I think Mr. Hannis had sought to indicate to the Court what pages the Prosecution wanted included in evidence, but you had asked that the matter be discussed with the Defence first. That has been done and it has been agreed with Mr. Ackerman, who was moving for the entry of certain pages. It has been agreed that in respect to the Prosecution the pages from the transcript are 1925 to 1933, 1940 to 1945, and 2032 to 2035 are to be included as evidence as extracts of the transcript from him testimony. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, in addition to what Mr. Ackerman had asked to be -- to be admitted. He had asked for 1928 to 32. We were basically asking for three pages before that as well, and one page after, to put it in context. He had asked for 1936 to 1931. He had for 1940 to 1942. We are asking it be 1940 to 1945. He had asked for page 2000, page 2045, page 2018, and page 2026. In respect to the last one we are asking in addition to page 2026 that page 2032 to 35 also be included. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. I take it your silence means you have nothing to add, Mr. Ackerman? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yesterday when you were being cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac, and we will resume that cross-examination now. I simply have to remind you that the solemn declaration to tell the truth which you took at the beginning of your evidence will continue to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, yesterday we interrupted our cross-examination when we were dealing with a particular topic -- or rather, something that happened on the 28th of March, 1999. Now I shall slowly -- well, actually, this has to do with the minaret of the mosque in Suva Reka. You confirmed to me - and once again I want to have the right context for my next questions. I'm going to read out part of your statement dated the 17th of August, 2001. I'm going to read about what you said then. "On the 28th of March around 1150 in the morning I heard an explosion and I saw the minaret destroyed. I rang a relative who lived near the mosque, who stated that the minaret had been blown up by the Serbs. That was on Bajram day and normally the mosque would have been full of Albanian people." And then you move on to 6.00 that evening. Another villager talking about another story. Later on at the Milosevic trial when you were cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic the question was as follows --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could we please have a reference, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say that you heard a loud explosion and -- I apologise for the transcript. The accused Milosevic is asking --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we please have a reference to the Milosevic transcript page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You heard that the minaret was destroyed at the mosque. Is that right? The page is 7456, lines 10, 11, 12, and 13. "A. Yes, on the 28th of March, 1999, sometime at around 1155 we heard a great explosion. And when we watched, looked at the minaret which is about 300 metres away, we saw that the minaret had gone. Meanwhile, in that five or six minutes' period on the road that leads towards Pristina, we saw a camouflage vehicle going towards Birac, which is 3 kilometres from Suva Reka where army forces were stationed. We saw that the minaret of the mosque in Suva Reka had been destroyed. That was the Bajram holiday which is a festival for Albanian Muslims." Then you move on to another topic. So this has to do with the very same incident. That is your second statement in which you made no reference to what you said yesterday during the direct examination by the Prosecution. When we checked the transcript, I will show you that actually yesterday you said two completely different things as well. The Prosecutor asked: [In English] "Did they tell you who they -- had they seen what had caused the explosion?" [Interpretation] Your answer was as follows: [In English] "There is a family, they are called Elshani, and they live very close to the mosque and they had seen the explosion and the collapse of the minaret. Fortunately, it did not fall on to their house, it fell on the other side, so it did not cause any damage to their house. At that time, they had seen a vehicle of the army, a Gazik it's called. It was a red vehicle. That was the only car that moved at that time. It went in the direction of Birac and it was a military vehicle." [Interpretation] In response to my question on the same day, but just a few minutes later you gave yet a fourth version of the same event and you said that your neighbours told you that they had seen this vehicle parked in front of the mosque. I don't know, Mr. Berisha, whether you understood that you are under oath, both when you're answering questions put by the Prosecution and the Defence. Could you please be so kind as to tell me which one of the four versions is correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, that is an impossible question to answer. They could well all be consistent with each other, you know. They may be incomplete. You have to take particular statements the witness has said and ask him whether it's true or not and build up a basis for saying that he's being inconsistent. You can't throw these four versions at him and expect him to give you an answer to the question you've just asked. Pick out two simple statements that you say are inconsistent with each other and ask him to explain it if there is an inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- yes, Your Honour. I'm going to ask him whether he stands by his claim made to the Prosecution during the examination-in-chief that this vehicle that they saw by the mosque was the only vehicle that was moving at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Only one vehicle was there at that time that went up in the direction of Birac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha. That's what we've been trying to hear from you since last night. Could you please be so kind as to tell us now, since you actually saw this vehicle and you said it was camouflaged, could you describe it for us?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This vehicle Gazik make of Russian manufacture had camouflage green colour. I did not say it was red. It had nuances of the green colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So it had different shades of green?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was camouflage with green pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Berisha, what would you say if I put it to you that the Army of Yugoslavia never had, not at that time either, a vehicle called Gazik or Gaz or any such vehicle that you described?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen such vehicles even earlier, the Gazik-type vehicles. This is what we called them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But they were not military vehicles, right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were military vehicles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And you saw them before the war, camouflage -- camouflage-coloured; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, do you perhaps know -- well, you heard the explosion, you saw the minaret fall. Do you know how the minaret was blown up? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I was in the courtyard, and at that moment we heard the explosion and we could no longer see the minaret. And now, after we reconstructed the minaret, I can still see it from my courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Just one more question with regard to this particular topic. Mr. Berisha, you said that on that day, Bajram day, the mosque was empty. Is there otherwise a janitor or some other person who takes care of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was completely empty, and it no longer had a janitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, now I am going to move on to my last topic very briefly. When was it that you returned to Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned on 23rd of June at 8.00 in the morning. I travelled throughout the night. So I arrived on the 23rd of June at 8.00 in the morning, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And when did you first enter the Municipal Assembly of Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became a co-chairman with the administrator on the 8th of October, 1999, but as a citizen I became member of the municipality even before this date. The 8th October is the date when the administrator designated my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Berisha, but you didn't understand me. I'm asking you when you first physically walked into the building of the municipality, not when you held a particular office.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date when I entered physically, but it was sometime in July. I don't remember the date, as I said. So up until July I did not enter physically the offices in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Oh, July. And the municipality building was held by UNMIK. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The municipality building right after the war was held by a temporary government, provisional government. It did not belong to UNMIK yet, but I wasn't there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So there was a provisional government and you were not there at the time, and when you came -- and then when you came there sometime in July after the provisional government, you found some papers in drawers. Did I understand you correctly? Did I understand your testimony correctly, the testimony you gave yesterday? These were papers from the Serb government that no one touched, the provisional government, UNMIK, no one by the month of July; is that what you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 8th of October, 1999, I was given the keys to the office by the administrator. Stanislav Andjelkovic, the chairman of the Executive Council of that government used to work in that office. As to whether someone entered that office before me, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And since you got these keys and found these things, did you take an inventory of the things that you found there by way of a commission or whatever, or did you just take them and put them away, as you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply took these documents, went through them. Those that I thought I might need, I took them with me and they were in my possession. And in the meantime, I was able to submit them to the archives of the Suhareke municipality. I have the originals at home, of the documents, I mean, that I presented here before you, while I handed over the copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Yes. That's what I asked you about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have some questions, and I hope that it's not menacing threat today after all these colleagues. I will try to cut it short as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Berisha. We'll briefly go back to page 30, line 9, concerning your response where you said that on the 8th of October, 1999, you were given the keys to the -- for the administrator, for your office. Is it correct that up until that day - and that is since June until the 8th of October - these offices were used by the PDK led by Hashim Thaqi, at least that's what is stated in the OSCE Mission to Kosovo report.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there was someone in those offices; however, the preparations to take up office and the post of the co-chairman of the administrative board, it was a period of a month and a half regular contacts with the UNMIK administrator appointed for Suhareke. He confirmed on the 6th of October that I had to report to the municipality building on the 8th of October to assume the post. And on this date he gave me the keys to the office --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question in the first few words. Just concentrate on what's being asked of you and confine the answer to that. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Berisha, do you have in front of you your statement in Albanian and do you need to have it to be able to refer to it?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you like to have it?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Albanian this is page 2, paragraph 1, and the same goes for the other two versions. You mention there the murder of the Berisha family. I wanted to tell you straight away that we are not going to dispute what you stated concerning that; we just wanted some clarification from you, if possible. Do you know who participated in these murders?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I didn't know, but I know now. Only when the survivors of this massacre were able to tell us. I spoke with my brother on the phone because I was not able to go to the petrol station. He was telling me that a massacre was being committed at the shopping centre, at the cafeteria called Kalebrija [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you were able to find out if some people from Suhareke participated in the murders?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that we learned now because I have the judgement of the war crimes court of Serbia, because only one of the perpetrators was not from Suhareke, he was from Nish, and the others were from Suhareke, Milorad Nisavic from Petkovic and Trajkovic families, I know all of them. And the Bosnian -- his name was Ramiz Papic or something like that. Now we've learned all the names but at that time we didn't know who committed the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from the members of your family, was anyone else killed in the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 49, including my brother who was killed later, are from the Berisha family from my neighbourhood. And there are others as well who were killed on the road to Rastane. This is what we call the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May we conclude that nobody from the surrounding houses, the houses which are adjacent to your relatives' house and immediately close by, that no one was killed from those houses?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The others were not killed. There were others as well there, but they were not killed. They were hiding in the basements of their houses, while out of the 49 that I mentioned 20 are less than 18 years old and then Hatixha [phoen] was 90 years old and Iri [phoen] who was pregnant and there was a 1-year-old child. I have the photographs of Hatixha here if you want to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe the Prosecutor will seek to tender some photographs through another witness who is to come here after you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you clarify something for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say -- is it the case that there is a judgement --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that there is an indictment at this point of time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not a judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not a judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I understand. Maybe the witness knows something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are the people indicted members of what can properly be described as the forces of the FRY or Serbia? [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Some of the individuals were, but I'm not sure because I don't have it with me. We are waiting, actually, Your Honour, for that indictment. Mr. Aleksic promised yesterday that we will have it today but we haven't received it yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, the people you mentioned, Milorad Nisavic, was he a member of any organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was chief of what we called Odba [phoen] the State Security Service in Suhareke. So he was chief of the state security office in Suhareke. I knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you then said -- or at least the transcript says from Petkovic and Trajkovic families. Now, who else are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two brothers, Zoran and Miki Petkovic. Miki is a nickname of one of the brothers; I don't know his name. They were brought up in Suhareke. We know them from their childhoods. I know their parents. His brother was a technician --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'd rather not -- [Previous translation continues] ... rather than their fathers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- have the indictment with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were they members of any organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They were just uniformed. I saw Miki wearing a uniform. I didn't see Zoran with uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Miki had a blue uniform, like the police uniform, the uniform with the blue nuances. Miki Petkovic. As I said, I don't know his full name, first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... matters to be explored further, no doubt the Prosecution will take it up with you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to conclude this topic, Mr. Berisha, and I will try and ask you to focus on the period before the 24th of March, 1999, a few days before that date. As a former municipal president and a resident of Suva Reka, were you familiar with the situation in and around the town at that time?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know it very well. First of all I would like to say that on the 22nd of March, in a shop a Serb was killed on the 22nd of March. The Serb was located at the old post office. It's a tall building, and the street behind the post office, 11 people were killed, one female and ten others. They were in their own houses and they had nothing to do with the assassination attempt. In the meantime, the situation was very bad. It was very difficult to go out in the street even before this date. My house, as I said yesterday, is on the other side of the road and it was really difficult for me to go on the other side. I didn't dare and nobody dared because the Serb police and military forces were moving along the main street. And some others that I mentioned yesterday, they were moving along that road as well, the ones with black uniforms and with the red bandannas. They were all linked to each other, and they were moving along the streets in Pinzgauers and in great speed, not a normal speed for that street. So whoever got caught, there was no way that he or she could escape, and these were all events that occurred even before the 25th and 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one question --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What, Mr. Berisha, is the link between the Serb who was killed on the 22nd of March and the 11 people that were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 11 persons that were killed had no connection whatsoever with the killing of the Serb. They were killed in their own house. This woman and ten other persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll adjourn there for the break and we'll resume just after five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I have from CLSS a memo following my request that they check the translation yesterday, and it reports as follows: "We confirm that the interpretation of the queried expression was inaccurate and that the English transcript page 3615, lines 14 to 16, should be corrected to read as follows: 'At that time, they had seen a vehicle of the army a Gazika in camouflage colours.'" So the word "red" was inaccurately added to that transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will be filed to correct the record. Mr. Lukic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, may we continue?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to those 11 people who were killed after Lazic Bogdan had been killed. Concerning that incident, was that a vendetta?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It was a vendetta because to this day we don't know where their bodies are. This was a macabre killing of civilians who were in no way involved with that killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I can ask only for one correction, only vendetta is translated but not blood feuding. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't know what you mean. Are you saying vendetta wasn't -- you didn't use the word vendetta?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did, both words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, you used both?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it has a specific meaning in that part of the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So your question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whether it was vendetta and blood feuding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to clarify something. As for Bogdan Lazic, you told us he was killed in Suva Reka. Did you know that the killing took place at around noon?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because my house is far from the shop where he worked, but the next day we learned that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for the members of your family, what was their relationship with the Nisics [as interpreted], who were owners of the hotel? It is well-known that people from the OSCE moved from the hotel to stay with your relatives.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think that they could have been -- that could have been one of the reasons because OSCE stayed there for a time, but they changed their offices because the citizens would not go to their offices because they knew that Misko worked for the state security. That's why the OSCE left the hotel and went to a private home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, one intervention regarding the transcript, and probably it would be corrected later on, but the correct last name of this person is Nisavic and the witness can confirm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Nisavic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does your answer mean you accept that the OSCE moved from a hotel, to which people were reluctant to go, to homes of members of the Berisha family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there rumours in the town as to who or what may have been the reason for the killing of some members of your family?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To this day we ask ourselves, because these families that were killed were honourable families, families who worked hard and did not have any conflict with anybody. All the families who were killed on the 26th of March, they were honest and hard-working families. The family of Sahit Berisha, where Musli was killed with 16 members of his family, they were an agricultural family, they were farmers. And one of them, Avdi and his wife, were in the clinic, and the others were all children. They had no conflict with anybody. Even the other families, they did not have any conflict with anyone. We could say something about the family of Vesel Berisha. There are two Vesel Berishas. There is Vesel Ramadan Berisha and Vesel Shaban Berisha. These families were killed. One of them was a professor at the university of Pristina. He taught at the civil engineering faculty. He was killed with his wife and two little children. Together with his sister, mother, and father. Ten members of that family were killed. Only two women survived. One is married in Suhareke, the other is married elsewhere. But as I said, all the families that were there, I don't know what the order was about this massacre, the killing, and who gave this order to put the whole family inside the cafeteria and explode the cafeteria -- they used detonators and stuff. That cafeteria is closed now. I don't know who that order came from. Those people behind you must know where this order came from. They have to explain. Why did they order this massacre? Well, mother Hatixha as we call her, she was almost a hundred years old and she was executed. And also Liri Berisha, who was pregnant, and there was an additional crime to this. There was insult to injury. They were first buried at Kroj i Popit and then exhumed and settle elsewhere. I don't know why they did that because I would think they want to hide their crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha. I only tried to ask you whether at the time there may have been any speculation as to the reason why your family members had been killed, but judging by your answer am I free to conclude that you have no knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were speculations. My brother was executed after the massacre happened just because he was working at the petrol station and because he was a witness; that was the reason, and he saw the crime. And he was executed between 5.00 and 6.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, again can you help me. Is the burial site that was referred to just now at Kroj i Popit, is that different from the firing range in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is always a confusion with these bilingual names. So we'll check it and provide you the answer as soon as possible or maybe the Prosecution can help us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, it was just if I could assist Your Honour. It's our understanding that it is the same location and the next witness will be giving more evidence on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Berisha, as someone who was familiar with the situation in Suva Reka, did you know that as of the 25th of March, 1999, there were skirmishes or conflicts between the KLA and the Serb forces? And I have in mind the area west to Suva Reka, between Velika Krusa and Rastani, that entire area was where the conflicts took place.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the centre of Suhareke there were no KLA soldiers, while 2 or 3 kilometres from Suhareke there were some. They were in Rastane, Doberdolan but not in the centre of Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in that area there were some 1500 members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was not in that area. I was on the other side of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph -- in the Albanian page 3, paragraph 2; in the English, page 2, paragraph 4; and in the B/C/S, page 2, paragraph 4, you state that they were shooting at the Albanians in the town. Do you know whether anyone was killed?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 25th of March, I said that a member from our family that lived on the other side of the street, they went out, and on that street brothers Hoti were killed, someone from the family Elshani, also someone named Suka. So 34 people were killed that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was actually the day when the fighting broke out between the KLA and the Serb forces. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The KLA was 3 kilometres away. There were no KLA in the town itself. There were only civilians in their own homes, and they were killed. Nebil Elshani [phoen] was killed in his own home, while the others that I mentioned were killed in the middle of town. The others were killed on the street, while the KLA forces were 3 kilometres away. There were no other people, no military people except those civilians who were in their own home.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness and counsel please wait for translation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stayed at home and I was taking care of my family. There were 18 members of my family that I had to take care of. I did not dare go out because I feared I would be killed. I stayed at home. But on the 25th we left, we left and went towards a river. The river is 500 metres from our home. We spent the day there, and you know the whole story; I have explained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Albanian page 3, paragraph 4; in the English, page 2, last paragraph; in the B/C/S page 3, paragraph 2, you state that on the 25th of March, 1999, around 6.30 a.m., between 20 and 30 members of the Kuci family passed by your house. Did they come from the direction of Rastani --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that was changed in the statement to between 20 and 30 members of the family Berisha, Ramadan Berisha --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they come from the direction of Rastani?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They crossed the main road. They live on the right side of the Pristina-Prizren road, so they crossed the road and they came towards the area where I lived, behind the municipality building. And there is this lane, as I told you, that divides the Serbs from the Albanians. And they left or went towards an area that is outside Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, we could see from your statement that there was looting and robbery in your town as well. Did you know that some people were later arrested for these crimes?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of March at around 4.00 p.m., on the road to Rastane there were houses where the massacre happened from where the people were taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you, please. The question is: Did you know that some people were later arrested for looting and robbery? Now, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one was arrested, Hamit Berisha, and he was released later because he was arrested by mistake. He was arrested on the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, just a few issues. You were asked whether or not anybody were killed -- anybody were killed -- any of your neighbours were killed on the 26th of March, and then you later talked about a number of killings that occurred on that day in Suva Reka. My question is: Is it a correct understanding of your evidence that there were other killings than the killing -- the big massacre of your relatives close to the petrol station, though those killings were not in your immediate neighbourhood. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were killings on the 22nd of March, 25th of March, 26th of March, and individual killings occurred up to the end of the war. The total number of the civilians killed, according to the statistics we have, it's 561 civilians. Of those, 176 civilians are unidentified and 152 from the municipality of Suhareke are still not found. Among those, 31 are from the Berisha family, people who have disappeared. We have not found them yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You say "statistics that we have," are you referring to anybody in particular who have collected these -- made these statistics?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I work with some other people in the association for missing persons and killed persons. And from the end of the war I joined this association and I worked there with Mr. Hysni Berisha. We have the statistics for the people who were killed in the commune in the municipality of Suhareke. The association is called Spreshimi [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Hysni Berisha will be a witness later in the trial, just so you are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you were asked whether you were -- you were asked about the people who are indicted before the Belgrade war crimes court. You were asked if you knew what organisation they belonged to. You explained that one of them was a policeman belonging to the state security and another one you described as -- as wearing a police uniform. Do you know whether any of the other accused belonged to -- were members of the army or the police or any unit like that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitrovic Radislav, from the indictment, I don't know him. Radamovic Radojko, he was commander of the police station in Suhareke. I knew him very well because he lived in Suhareke for a long time. Jovanovic Nenad, I know him as well. He was the deputy police commander in Suhareke police station. He was an active policeman. Cukaric Sladjan. Nisavic Milorad, he worked at the state security. He was chief of the office in Suhareke. I know him very well because during the time I served as the chairman of the municipality in 1989/1991 he worked there and had the same function. Petkovic Miroslav and Petkovic Zoran, they were civilians before the war. One of them, Zoran, worked as a driver, while Petkovic Miroslav for a time worked in the office of the health care, and the person with a last name Papic, he was an active policeman as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, what document were you reading from just now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading these names from the indictment issued by the office of the Prosecutor at the war crimes court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that an exhibit, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It is not an exhibit, and obviously the witness has a copy of the indictment. We also have a translation of the indictment that we can offer to the Court if the Court is -- would find that helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't interest you then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We will be leading more evidence about the identity of these people from other witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- Witness K83 who will come next week --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right thank you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- will provide more information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You were being asked whether there had been an incident of a vendetta and a blood feud, and my learned colleague stated that that had a specific meaning in the region. I don't know if it's being suggested that these killings were the result of a vendetta or a feud, but just to cover this, Mr. Berisha, the killings that occurred in March through May 1999 in Suva Reka, have you any indications that they were a result of vendettas and blood feuds?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's act of revenge. There's no vendetta or blood feud between the Serb and Albanian community; it's only revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So these are different concepts. What do you mean by "revenge"?
